about.title: Our mission is clarity.
about.description: We believe understanding your health should not require a medical degree. Health Made Clear is dedicated to translating complex medical language into plain, actionable language so more people can make informed decisions.
about.valueEducationBody: The content in Health Made Clear is strictly educational and informational. It is designed to support conversations with healthcare professionals, not replace them.
about.valueEveryoneBody: From high-contrast colors to readable typography and printable tools, every part of the platform is designed to be easier to use.
about.valueStructuredBody: Information is organized into guided paths and short lessons so people can build confidence without overload.
about.warningBody: Never disregard professional medical advice or delay seeking it because of something you read here. If you think you may have a medical emergency, call your doctor or emergency services immediately.
about.contactBody: Questions or feedback? Reach us at
about.whyMattersBody: Low health literacy is linked to poorer outcomes, higher healthcare costs, and more frequent hospitalizations. Clearer education can help people prepare, ask better questions, and follow care plans more confidently.
about.educationDetail: The content provided on Health Made Clear is for educational purposes only. It is meant to make health information easier to understand and support patient confidence.
about.joinBody: Improving health literacy is a community effort. Whether you are a clinician reviewing content for accuracy, a designer improving usability, or a patient sharing lived experience, your contribution matters.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.description: How we handle your information at Health Made Clear.
privacy.educationBody: Health Made Clear is an educational resource. We do not provide medical diagnoses or treatments. Quiz answers and lesson progress are learning data about health topics, not medical records.
privacy.collectBody: What we store depends on how you use the site: as a guest, with an account, through Contact, or via analytics and crash reporting.
privacy.collectBodyGuest: Anonymous use: progress and preferences stay in the browser (localStorage / cookies). We do not create an account unless you sign up. Leftover progress on this device can attach to whoever signs in next on a shared computer.
privacy.collectBodyAccount: If you create an account, we store on our database (Supabase, United States): display name, email (Auth), lesson completion, quiz scores and answers, streaks, daily activity dates, and in-app notifications. This syncs progress across devices.
privacy.collectBodyContact: If you use Contact, we store your name, email, subject, and message to respond. These messages are not linked to a learning account. Deleting your account does not delete contact messages you already sent. To request deletion of a submitted message, email {privacyEmail}.
privacy.collectBodyAnalytics: We use Google Analytics for page views. We send the page path (which can include lesson or article slugs — topics you opened), not your name, and not search-box text. Google Analytics 4 does not store IP addresses. This app sends path only (origin + pathname). We do not send the URL query string or hash. Analytics cookies (_ga, _gid, _ga_*) stay on the device until logout/delete expires them, or until you clear site data — on a shared device they can keep a client id across visitors until then.
privacy.collectBodyErrors: If crash reporting is enabled, we may receive the page path (including lesson or article slugs) and a technical error message. We do not send your name, email, or IP address in those reports. We strip URL query strings and hash fragments (the part after #).
privacy.controlBody: Signed-in: Dashboard → Settings to delete your account (auth user + learning data). Guests: clear site data in the browser. You can export progress from the Dashboard.

tools.careGuideDescription: This page explains what home care, clinics, urgent care, and emergency departments often do. It cannot choose a place for you.
tools.homeCareBody: Home care often means rest and fluids while mild symptoms improve. Speak with a clinician or pharmacist before taking an over-the-counter medicine, especially for children, pregnancy, or chronic conditions. This page cannot tell you which medicine is right for you.
tools.primaryCareBody: Primary care clinics often handle checkups, ongoing conditions, and symptoms that are not emergencies. They can help you plan next steps with a clinician. This page cannot assign you a clinic or a diagnosis.
tools.urgentCareBody: Urgent-care clinics often treat problems that need same-day attention but are not life-threatening — for example sprains or a moderate fever. That is what those clinics often do, not an instruction for your symptoms.
tools.emergencyBody: Emergency departments treat life-threatening physical problems such as severe chest pain, trouble breathing, stroke signs, and heavy bleeding. For a mental health crisis or thoughts of self-harm in the United States, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline). This page cannot decide whether you must go to an emergency department.
tools.homeCareChecklist: Mild cold symptoms|Minor cuts or scrapes|Muscle aches from exercise
tools.homeCarePediatricNote: A temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in an infant under 3 months is treated as an emergency in US emergency departments — not as home monitoring. Get emergency care now, or call the pediatrician immediately. Call 911 if the baby is hard to wake, is having trouble breathing, or you cannot get to emergency care. In babies and children under 3, watch for no tears when crying, a sunken soft spot on the head, fewer than 6 wet diapers in 24 hours if they still use diapers, or no urine for 8 hours. In older children, dark urine, dry mouth, or dizziness means call a clinician — not 911 by itself. At any age, if a child is hard to wake or not drinking, call 911 in the United States.
tools.primaryCareChecklist: Annual checkups|Ongoing conditions|New symptoms lasting several days|Prescription refill visits
tools.urgentCareChecklist: Sprains or minor fractures|Stitches for small cuts|Moderate fever|Urinary tract infection symptoms
tools.emergencyChecklist: Chest pain or pressure|Trouble breathing|Stroke signs (FAST)|Severe bleeding or head injury
tools.scenarioNotAdvice: These examples describe common care settings. They are not a clinical recommendation for your symptoms.
tools.scenarioSoreThroatBody: Most mild sore throats are evaluated in primary care or a nurse line. This page cannot tell you what you have. Severe trouble swallowing, drooling, inability to open the mouth, or trouble breathing are emergencies — in the United States, call 911.
tools.scenarioChestPainTitle: Chest pain and related warning signs
tools.scenarioChestPainBody: A heart attack can cause many different symptoms — not just crushing chest pain. Warning signs include jaw, neck, back, or arm pain, sudden shortness of breath, unexplained cold sweats, nausea, or dizziness. These symptoms may be more common in women, older adults, and people with diabetes, but anyone can experience them. If you notice any of these symptoms, do not wait and do not self-treat. In the United States, call 911 immediately.
tools.whenInDoubtBody: If you think you may be having an emergency, use local emergency services. In the United States that is 911. For a mental health crisis or thoughts of self-harm in the United States, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline). For questions about accidental double doses, medicine mix-ups, or suspected poisoning in the United States, call Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222 (free, confidential, 24/7). If the person collapsed, is not breathing, or is having a seizure, call 911 first. This site cannot tell you how serious your symptoms are or where you should go.
tools.printEmergencyLine: For medical emergencies, call 911. For mental health crises, call or text 988 (US).
tools.printFooter: Printed from Health Made Clear (healthmadeclear.com) on {date}. Educational content — not a substitute for clinical diagnosis or individualized medical advice. For emergencies, call 911 (US).
